name: Rafael Khan

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government, and everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm field manager for Dunmore Growers. We grow leeks, cabbages, cauliflower and carrots for two of the big supermarkets, about four hundred hectares. Right now it's leek harvest, so I'm in the field at six with the crew, twenty-five people on the harvester rig, trimming and packing in the rain. Then I'm on the phone to the pack-house, because the supermarket wants a thousand more boxes than yesterday, or a thousand fewer. My old pickup has a hundred and ninety thousand on the clock and smells of leeks, permanently.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: A good crew on a good day. When the rig's moving, everyone's quick and laughing, and we fill the lorry by two. My father worked on this same farm when he first came to this country, picking by hand. Now I run it. That means something to me.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The supermarket. They change the order at nine at night, they reject a whole load because the leeks are two centimetres too long, and we eat the cost. And the pay, I earn less than the managers at the bigger growers. But with Samira's job at the school kitchen and the kids settled, I'm not moving. We have maybe three weeks' money put by. That's it.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Do you use any technology yourself?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The rig has its own computer, and the owner's son runs the planting plans on a laptop. Me, I've got a phone for calls and that's enough. I've never used one of these AI things and I don't want to. My father said a man should be able to do his job with his own head.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. Picture this. AI stays a handy tool, like a better search engine. Hiring, pay and prices carry on the way they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good for the people in offices, and leave us out of it. At the rig the crew wouldn't care. Half of them would say their kids use it to cheat at school, and they'd be right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing. It means nothing for me. My problems are the supermarket, the weather, and finding twenty-five people who'll stand in a wet field in November. A computer that answers questions doesn't fix any of that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as every year. Get the leeks out, get the crew paid, pray for a dry spring. Maybe I'd tell Yusuf not to use it for his homework, and he'd ignore me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's somebody else's business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said finding twenty-five people. How hard is that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Harder every year. The young men from the town don't want it, they'd rather sit on benefits than get wet, some of them. Most of my crew come from abroad for the season, like my father did. Good workers, every one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd pray for a dry spring. Is faith a big part of how you get through a year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It is. Friday prayers, every week, even in harvest. My boss knows I go and he lets me. You can't control the weather or the supermarket, so you do your best and leave the rest to God.

S0.say: I'd say good for the office people, and leave us out of it. The crew wouldn't care, and half would say their kids use it to cheat at school.
S0.think: I think it means nothing for me. My problems are the supermarket, the weather and finding twenty-five people for a wet field, and a question-answering computer fixes none of them.
S0.do: Carries on as usual, getting the leek harvest in, paying the crew and praying for a dry spring. Tells his son not to use AI for homework, expecting to be ignored.
S0.feel: Calm, because it's somebody else's business.
S0.quote: You can't control the weather or the supermarket, so you do your best and leave the rest to God.
S0.fieldNote: He frames life around work, family and faith, and is proud that his father once picked on the farm he now runs. He's sharp about young local men avoiding the work while praising seasonal workers. AI simply isn't in his world yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks. Here's the second. Now picture this. Very capable AI exists, but it spreads slowly, over ten years or more. Some tasks disappear, but few whole jobs do. Companies hire fewer beginners. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say if the big companies stop taking on young people, that's their mistake, and the country will pay for it. Young people need to start at the bottom and learn the trade. That's how I did it, that's how my father did it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think it reaches me through the supermarket. They'll have some system that predicts orders and checks quality from photos, and they'll use it to reject more loads and pay less. They're already hard to deal with, and this makes them harder.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much. Keep doing the job right, keep the quality high so they've got no excuse to reject. I'd tell the owner to get his son to deal with their computers, that's his side. I'd keep my side, the field and the crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A bit annoyed, like when it rains on a Saturday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said young people need to start at the bottom. Would you want Yusuf on the rig?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For a summer, yes. It'd do him good. But not for a life. I want him to be an engineer, or a pharmacist, something with letters after his name. My father wanted the same for me and I ended up in the field anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The owner's son runs the computer side. How do you two get on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine, as long as he doesn't tell me how to harvest leeks. He's a good lad, clever. But he sees the field on a screen. I see it with my boots.

S1.say: I'd say if big companies stop taking on young people, that's their mistake and the country will pay. Young people need to start at the bottom and learn the trade, as my father and I did.
S1.think: I think it reaches me through the supermarket, using systems to predict orders and judge quality from photos. They'd reject more loads and pay less, making them even harder to deal with.
S1.do: Keeps quality high so the supermarket has no excuse to reject loads. Leaves the computer side to the owner's son and keeps his own focus on the field and the crew.
S1.feel: Calm, a bit annoyed, like rain on a Saturday.
S1.quote: He's a good lad, clever. But he sees the field on a screen. I see it with my boots.
S1.fieldNote: His traditional views come through as respect for starting at the bottom and earning your way. He wants more for his son than the field, which echoes his own father. He draws a firm line between his work and the screen work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the third picture. Next one. Within 5 years, AI assistants that can act on their own handle most routine office work. There are layoffs and pay pressure in office jobs. Some new AI-related jobs appear, and politicians argue loudly about what to do. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the government should stay out of it and let people find new work, the way people always have. Paying people to sit at home is the wrong answer. Apprenticeships, yes. Handouts, no.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think it gets closer. The pack-house has an office of eight, doing the orders and the paperwork with the supermarket. If those go to a machine, the owner saves money, fine. But my cousin Imran is one of them, and he's got three kids.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try to get Imran onto the field side, as my deputy, before the office cuts come. He'd hate the rain but he'd have a job. I'd also stop the satellite TV, that's about thirty a month, and put it aside. And I'd tell Samira to ask the school about more hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's not me yet, but it's my family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said handouts, no. If Imran couldn't find anything, would you still say that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's hard. I'd want him to take any work going, even picking. If there was nothing, really nothing, then the family would help first, like we always have. The government last. I know that sounds old-fashioned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Imran?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him to come and see me at six on Monday, in old boots. He'd laugh. Then he'd come, because he's not a man who sits at home.

S2.say: I'd say the government should stay out of it and let people find new work as they always have. Paying people to sit at home is wrong, so apprenticeships yes, handouts no.
S2.think: I think it's getting closer, since the pack-house office of eight could be replaced by a machine. My cousin Imran works there and has three kids.
S2.do: Tries to bring his cousin Imran onto the field side as his deputy before office cuts, cancels satellite TV to save about thirty a month, and asks his partner to seek more hours at the school.
S2.feel: Uneasy, because it's touching his family even if not him yet.
S2.quote: I'd tell him to come and see me at six on Monday, in old boots.
S2.fieldNote: When pressed on handouts, he held his line but softened it: family first, government last. His instinct is to find his cousin work, not money. The image of the six o'clock Monday start shows how he thinks help should look.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the fourth. Now a faster version. Within 2 to 3 years, AI matches skilled professionals at most thinking work. Lots of office and professional workers lose their jobs. Share and house prices boom. There's a political crisis over who should get the gains. Physical jobs are mostly untouched. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people who own shares and houses earned them, mostly, and taking them away isn't the answer. But I'd also say something's wrong if men who worked all their lives are out of a job while others get rich doing nothing. I don't have a neat answer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'm safe, my work's in the mud. But the house prices, that's bad for us. We have a mortgage and nothing saved. When Yusuf and Amina grow up, they'll never buy a house round here. And all those office people out of work, some of them will come looking for field work, and they won't last a week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep my head down and work. Take every hour of overtime in the harvest. I'd ask the owner for a small rise, because if the supermarket is selling more cheap veg to people with less money, we're busier. And I'd put the overtime money aside, all of it, even if it's only a few hundred.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. The world is going wrong somewhere, and I'm in a field watching it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said office people would come for field work and not last a week. Why so sure?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I've seen it. During the pandemic we had a whole crew of students and office workers. Good people, but by Thursday half had gone. Your back has to learn this work, it takes a season.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You don't have a neat answer on sharing the gains. If you had to pick one thing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Make it easier to start a business and to hire young people. Less paperwork, less tax on the small man. The big companies always find a way, it's the small ones who drown.

S3.say: I'd say people mostly earned their shares and houses, and taking them isn't the answer. But something's wrong when lifelong workers lose jobs while others get rich doing nothing, and I have no neat answer.
S3.think: I think I'm safe since my work is in the mud. But booming house prices hurt a family with a mortgage and no savings, my children won't afford a home here, and laid-off office workers won't last in the field.
S3.do: Keeps his head down, takes all harvest overtime and saves every penny of it, and asks the owner for a small rise since cheap vegetables would sell more.
S3.feel: Uneasy, watching the world go wrong from a field.
S3.quote: Your back has to learn this work, it takes a season.
S3.fieldNote: He holds free-market views but is honestly troubled by unearned wealth, and says he doesn't have a neat answer. When pressed, he went back to helping small businesses. His pandemic memory about office workers in the field was vivid and specific.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the last one. Last one. Everything in the previous picture happens, and on top of that, general-purpose robots arrive in warehouses, kitchens, building sites, farms and care homes within 3 to 5 years. Hands-on work is no longer a safe place to be. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this isn't progress, it's foolishness. A country that can't grow its own food without machines from a factory abroad is weak. I'd say it at the growers' meeting, and I'd say it at the mosque, where half the men work with their hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, vegetables are going to be first. They already have machines that see a weed and zap it, and cameras that sort carrots. A robot that cuts a cauliflower is coming. The owner would buy them the day they're cheaper than a crew, and then he doesn't need twenty-five people, and he doesn't need a man to run twenty-five people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know. I'm not going to learn to fix robots at forty-three, I'm not built for it. I'd ask the owner to keep me as long as there's work, and save every penny. Maybe ask around the bigger growers, but they'd be doing the same. Samira would have to work full time, and I'd hate that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Like the night before a hard frost, when the crop's still in the ground and there's nothing you can do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd hate Samira working full time. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'm supposed to provide. That's how I was raised. She'd say it's nonsense, and maybe it is, but it's in my bones. It would feel like I'd failed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You won't learn to fix robots. If the owner offered it to you, with training, would you still say no?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe I'd try. For the kids, I'd try. But I'd be a man pressing buttons on a screen in a field where my father picked by hand. I don't know what that would do to me.

S4.say: I'd say this isn't progress but foolishness, because a country that can't grow food without imported machines is weak. I'd say it at the growers' meeting and at the mosque, where many men do hands-on work.
S4.think: I think vegetables go first, with weeding machines and carrot-sorting cameras already here and cauliflower-cutting robots coming. The owner would buy them once cheaper than a crew, and wouldn't need a crew manager either.
S4.do: Refuses to retrain on robots at first, asks the owner to keep him as long as possible and saves every penny. Asks around bigger growers and expects his partner to go full time, which he'd hate.
S4.feel: Alarmed, like the night before a hard frost with the crop still in the ground.
S4.quote: But I'd be a man pressing buttons on a screen in a field where my father picked by hand.
S4.fieldNote: His sense of being the provider was the strongest feeling in the interview, and he admitted it might be old-fashioned. He first refused to retrain, then said he might try for his children. The link to his father's labour on the same land gives the loss real weight.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The robots, no question. The rest I can work through. That one takes the work away, and work is what I am. What would help is apprenticeships for men my age, real ones, paid, on a farm, not a classroom. And for the government to back growers who keep people on, not just the ones who buy the most machines.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the crews. Twenty-five people come every year from three countries, and they send money home to their families. If the robots come, it's not just me, it's villages I've never seen. Nobody talks about them.

headlineQuote: But I'd be a man pressing buttons on a screen in a field where my father picked by hand. I don't know what that would do to me.
portrait: Rafael Khan, 43, is field manager at Dunmore Growers, running a twenty-five-person harvest crew on vegetables for two supermarkets, on the same farm where his father once picked by hand. He never uses AI, believes in hard work, family help and apprenticeships over handouts, and draws strength from his faith. Through the early scenarios he feels his work in the mud is safe and worries instead about his cousin's office job and his children's chances of owning a house. In the robot scenario he expects vegetable growing to automate first and struggles with the idea of no longer being the provider.
biggestWorry: The robot scenario, because it would take away the work that he feels defines him, starting with vegetable farms.
whatWouldHelp: Paid, farm-based apprenticeships for men his age, and government backing for growers who keep people on rather than buying the most machines.
